sources.citation: Jackson, Eric M. 2019. Two-part negation in Yang Zhuang. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 12(1).
sources.note: Silent; footnote 9 gives the Yang Zhuang phonemic transcription conventions and tone sandhi (fn 18) only.
sources.venue: Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society

sources.citation: Jackson, Emily H. S., Eric M. Jackson & Lau Shuh Huey. 2012. A sociolinguistic survey of the Dejing Zhuang dialect area. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2012-036. 168 pp.
sources.note: Silent: no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' in the linguistic sense (Yang / Min Zhuang tone and segment notes only).

sources.citation: Johnson, Eric C. 2011. A lexical and phonological comparison of the Central Taic languages of Wenshan Prefecture, China: getting more out of language survey wordlists than just lexical similarity percentages. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-005. Dallas: SIL International. 150 pp.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Ch. 3 'Comparative Phonology' (pp. 14-117) covers Nong, Dai and Min Zhuang tone systems, consonants and vowels only; sec. 3.6 (p. ~110) concedes 'a full phonology would, of course, also include treatment of non-Taic loanwords, allophony (including tone sandhi), morphophonology, intonation, etc.' No occurrence of 'stress' except a non-linguistic use.

sources.citation: Johnson, Eric C. 2010. A sociolinguistic introduction to the Central Taic languages of Wenshan Prefecture, China. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2010-027.
sources.note: Silent; 'accent' occurs only in the sense of regional pronunciation in intelligibility-test discussion.

sources.citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. 2009. The phonology of Proto-Tai. Ph.D. dissertation, Cornell University.
sources.note: Comparative/historical only: claims Proto-Tai prosodic words were monosyllables or sesquisyllables each containing 'exactly one iambic foot headed by a heavy syllable' (ch. 2); no synchronic statement about stress in any Southern Zhuang variety.

sources.citation: Luo Yongxian. 2008. Zhuang. In Anthony Diller, Jerold A. Edmondson & Luo Yongxian (eds.), The Tai-Kadai languages, 317-377. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Silent. Phonology sketch (9.2) is of Fengshan, a Northern Zhuang variety; six tones; 'The majority of words in Zhuang are monosyllabic.. Disyllabic words are not uncommon.' No mention of stress or accent; Southern Zhuang is treated only in the tone-comparison table 9.2-4.

sources.citation: Wang Mingfu & Eric Johnson. 2008. 壮族文化遗产及壮语研究 / Zhuang cultural and linguistic heritage. Kunming: Yunnan Nationalities Publishing House. 227 pp.
sources.note: Table of contents inspected (pp. 1-2 rendered): part IV 'Zhuang language research in Wenshan' (pp. 129-167) has dialect-group, vocabulary, contact, intelligibility, vitality and orthography sections but no phonology chapter; not scanned, no stress statement expected.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority (submitter Eric C. Johnson). 2006/2007. Change Request 2006-128: split of Southern Zhuang [ccy] into [zhd] [zhn] [zyg] [zyn] [zzj]. SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing; administrative document. Its 'Sources of information' section (pp. 3-4) lists the Chinese descriptions: Zhang Junru et al. 1999 壮语方言研究; Zhang Yuansheng & Wei Xingyun 1997 in Comparative Kadai: the Tai branch; Yan Shangyue (ed.) 1994 壮语方言土语音系; Wei Qingwen & Tan Guosheng 1979/1980 壮语简志; Zheng Yiqing 1996 靖西方言研究; Edmondson 1984.

sources.citation: Hudak, Thomas J. (ed.). 1995. William J. Gedney's Central Tai dialects: glossaries, texts, and translations (Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 43). Introductions to the Tai dialects of Lei Ping (p. 117ff.) and Ping Siang, Rosetta Project scans rosettaproject_ccy_phon-2 / phon-3.
sources.note: Silent. Each introduction: 'shows distinctions in syllable-initial consonant, in vocalic nucleus, in syllable-final consonant, and in tone', followed by tone inventories (Lei Ping 5, Ping Siang 6 tones) and tone-split tables; nothing on stress.
sources.venue: Introductions to the Tai dialects of Lei Ping

sources.citation: Gedney, William J. (ed. Thomas J. Hudak). 1991. William J. Gedney's The Tai dialect of Lungming: glossary, texts, and translations (Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 39). Ann Arbor: Center for South and Southeast Asian Studies. Pages xix-xxviii ('Phonology') as scanned by the Rosetta Project.
sources.note: Silent. p. xix: 'the phonological pattern of Lungming is based on the syllable. Each syllable has distinctions in tone, initial.., nucleus.. and optional final consonant.' Then six tones (Chao values), tone-split table, initials, vowels, rhymes chart. No word on stress/accent. (Full volume is HathiTrust search-only, mdp.39015028428467.)
sources.venue: Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 39
